paper_title: How Complete Must an Environment Be to Train a Capable GUI Agent?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are widely trained in executable GUI environments. To lower cost, build environments in batches, and reduce manual effort, each work trades away part of the environment through its construction choices. We describe these choices along three dimensions: reward coverage, the goal-reaching trajectories the verifier rewards; data coverage, the application data the agent is exposed to beyond what the task reads or writes; and feature coverage, the application features beyond what the task uses. Existing works set each dimension on engineering grounds, but they do not measure its effect on training. How complete must an environment be to train a capable agent, and along which dimensions? In MobileGym, we adjust each dimension separately, train Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, and evaluate every policy in the original full environment. A verifier that rewards only one reference path lowers success by 10.53 points, and removing unneeded records also lowers success. Pruning unneeded features instead raises success from 51.61% to 56.13%, entirely on tasks whose environments it left unchanged. The gain reverses when each episode is weighted equally and vanishes when only episodes on the pruned tasks are balanced. Without pruning, length weighting there reinforces long detour successes that erode skills on other tasks. Following these findings, we build MobileGym-Lite, which keeps reward and data coverage complete and prunes unneeded features. It outperforms Full in the full environment (55.48% versus 51.61% success) with lower construction cost.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are widely trained in executable GUI environments. To lower cost, build environments in batches, and reduce manual effort, each work trades away part of the environment through its construction choices. We describe these choices along three dimensions: reward coverage, the goal-reaching trajectories the verifier rewards; data coverage, the application data the agent is exposed to beyond what the task reads or writes; and feature coverage, the application features beyond what the task uses. Existing works set each dimension on engineering grounds, but they do not measure its effect on training. How complete must an environment be to train capable agent, and along which dimensions? In MobileGym, we adjust each dimension separately, train Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, and evaluate every policy in the original full environment. verifier that rewards only one reference path lowers success by 10.53 points, and removing unneeded records also lowers success. Pruning unneeded features instead raises success from 51.61% to 56.13%, entirely on tasks whose environments it left unchanged. The gain reverses when each episode is weighted equally and vanishes when only episodes on the pruned tasks are balanced. Without pruning, length weighting there reinforces long detour successes that erode skills on other tasks. Following these findings, we build MobileGymLite, which keeps reward and data coverage complete and prunes unneeded features. It outperforms Full in the full environment (55.48% versus 51.61% success) with lower construction cost. 1. Introduction Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are increasingly trained and evaluated in executable GUI environments. Benchmarks such as WebArena, VisualWebArena, AndroidWorld, and OSWorld check task completion through interaction [6, 13, 25, 33], and growing line of work trains agents inside such environments with reinforcement learning or synthesized experience [1, 3, 12, 15, 24]. Building these environments is costly, so each work makes its own construction choices, trading part of the environment for lower cost, batch automation, and less manual effort. Therefore, we ask: how complete must GUI environment be to train capable GUI agent, and along which dimensions? We describe construction choices along three dimensions  (Fig. 1)  . Viewing the environment as partially observable Markov decision process, the builder writes verifier that defines the reward, fills the applications with data that form different states, and implements the features that define the transitions. Reward coverage is how many goal-reaching trajectories the verifier rewards. Data coverage is how much application data the agent is exposed to beyond the records the task reads or writes. Feature coverage is how many application features it implements beyond those the task uses. Existing works sacrifice each dimension to reduce construction cost. On reward, some choose to match actions step by step against reference trajectory or to train offline on annotated actions, which gives dense reward that is cheap to compute [5, 11, 30]. On data, some synthesize environments with few generated records instead of realistic application contents, which lowers cost and avoids copying real user or copyrighted content: GUI-GENESIS fills choice list with as few as three to five plausible but incorrect options [3], and ScaleWoB starts from minimal environment with seed records [9]. On features, builder can choose to implement only the functions that tasks use most, which shortens construction. For example, GUI-GENESIS implements only the logic that each tasks interactions require [3]. We answer this question in MobileGym [24]. Keeping task instructions and native goal checks fixed, we adjust one dimension at time: single-path reward lowers reward cov1 can omit features the task does not need but should keep reward and data coverage relatively complete. Following this strategy, we build MobileGym-Lite. It omits 87 templatemodule pairs across 72 of 192 training templates, removing 14.05% of the application source lines per pruned task on average, while keeping nearby navigation. Lite reaches 55.48% success in the full environment, 3.87 points above Full. Our contributions are threefold. (1) We propose the first three-dimensional taxonomy of completeness in GUI environment construction: reward coverage, data coverage, and feature coverage. We measure how lowering each affects training and explain the result with mechanism experiment. (2) We derive construction strategy from these findings as methodology for building GUI environments. (3) We build MobileGym-Lite with this strategy, and it trains stronger agent than the full environment. 2. Related Work GUI agents and their training. Executable benchmarks and platforms evaluate web, Android, and desktop agents through interaction [6, 13, 18, 25, 27, 33]. Reinforcement learning in such environments trains device-control and GUI agents [1, 12, 19, 21, 28, 29], and MobileGym provides browser-hosted mobile applications with programmable state and parallel rollouts for this purpose [24]. We use its editable application logic to adjust each construction dimension during training and restore the full environment for evaluation. On the objective side, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) normalizes rewards within sampled group [14], and Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) applies sequence-level importance ratios and clipping [32]. Prior work identifies token-length bias in reasoning-model optimization [10]. GUI interaction adds level of aggregation: one episode contains several model responses, each with several tokens. We reweight responses per episode while keeping the within-response objective, and test how this weighting changes the effect of functional pruning. and construction Environment reduction. GUIGENESIS synthesizes task-specific environments with executable reward assertions and compares them with real applications [3], OS-Genesis derives tasks from exploration of existing environments [15], and ScaleWoB co-generates related tasks to keep synthesized applications usable beyond one scripted path [9]. Other works replace real applications with LLM-simulated, virtual, or mock ones [16, 17, 20, 22, 26]. On the evaluation side, LlamaTouch and MobiBench show that single-path matching misjudges valid executions and accept multiple paths through essential states or per-step branches [5, 30], recent verifiers check goal-state anchors or probe the final state [4, 23, 31], whereas offline RL still rewards Figure 1. Three dimensions of GUI environment construction. Top: reward coverage. verifier rewards long-press deletion but not an edit-sheet solution that reaches the same goal. Middle: data coverage. R0/R1/R2 retain the records the task needs and vary the unrelated ones. Bottom: feature coverage. Full/F0/F1 expose different application functions. Policies train in the reduced environments and are evaluated in Full. erage, record filtering lowers data coverage, and functional pruning lowers feature coverage. We train Qwen3-VL-4BInstruct [2] in each variant and evaluate every policy in the original full environment (Full). We find that lowering reward or data coverage trains worse agent. Lowering feature coverage trains better one, and the gain comes from tasks whose environments pruning left unchanged. further experiment traces this gain to how the objective weights episodes by length. Balancing every episode reverses the gain, and balancing only the episodes on pruned tasks removes it, whereas balancing only successes or only failures leaves it intact. Without pruning, long successes that detour through unneeded functions carry heavy weight, and the shared policy loses tasks it already solves to loops. Pruning removes these detours. These findings give construction strategy: builder 2 agreement with one annotated action [11]. Data scale and device configuration also change how UI agents generalize [7, 8]. These works compare whole construction pipelines, evaluation rules, or data scale. We hold the applications and tasks fixed and lower reward coverage, data coverage, and feature coverage one at time, so each outcome can be attributed to one dimension. 3. Study Design 3.1. Environment Model and Controlled Variants Environment model. We model GUI environment as POMDP (S, A, T, R, Ω). state holds the application data and interface state. The policy receives only screenshot = Ω(s) and emits GUI action A, and is the applications response. task specifies an instruction x, an initial state s0, and native goal check Vx, from which is derived. builder authors three parts per task, each defining one dimension: the verifier defines R, the application data form s0, and the features define . Ω renders the state and is fixed by the device. Controlled variants. Each experiment group adjusts one dimension, keeps the other two as in Full, and is evaluated with the original R, records, and functions. The reduction is assigned per task template, family of instructions and initial states instantiated by seed, so the rule stays fixed as task instances vary. Each reduction is built not to reach into the other dimensions. Separate manipulations need not have separate effects: one policy learns all templates, so reduction on some tasks can change behavior on others, which the grouped evaluation in Sec. 3.3 measures. 3.2. Coverage Dimensions and Their Adjustment Reward coverage. Reward coverage is how many goalreaching trajectories, those that carries from s0 to state satisfying Vx, receive reward. To lower it, we restrict reward to reference operation sequence cx: rpath(τ, x) = 1[Vx(τ ) = 1] 1[M (τ, cx) = 1], (1) where matches ordered semantic operations, route, and target identity, with limited motor fallbacks. One reference covers each training template. Private DOM annotations identify operations for matching, while the policy observes only screenshots (Appendix B). The group keeps s0 and : all actions remain reachable and divergence leaves the episode running, so every route stays executable and only the set of rewarded paths shrinks. This is how reference-matching procedures lower reward coverage in practice: trajectory can satisfy the goal and still receive zero reward. Data coverage. Data coverage is how many records the environment holds beyond those the task reads or writes, such as unrelated alarms or messages. Record filtering lowers it: R0, R1, and R2 retain protected records and at most zero, one, or two unrelated records per reviewed list, changing 78 of the 192 training templates. Protected records cover both branches of conditional instruction, answer-relevant records, alternative entrances, and shared helpers. Retained rows keep their order and identities. The group keeps and . Because it protects every record solution reads or writes, every route to the goal and every function on the retained rows remain. Feature coverage. Feature coverage is how many functions, operations in whose controls Ω renders, the environment implements beyond those the task uses, such as the stopwatch. Functional pruning lowers it with task-specific masks that disable dispensable function modules, such as the stopwatch or Moments. F0 disables all reviewed dispensable modules for template, while F1 retains K/2 of its candidate modules by stable hash. F0 affects 78 templates, with 127 templatemodule disablements across Clock, Notes, Calendar, and WeChat. Masks keep function whenever the task needs it: alarm tasks lose the world-clock entrance while world-time tasks retain it. Cross-application tasks combine profile rules and protect shared helpers, and replay and state checks verify the retained operations. Templates without reviewed rule use Full, and Appendix lists all nine profiles. 3.3. Experimental Setup Training. We train Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct on dedicated MobileGym research split. pass comprises 16 outer steps of 12 tasks and eight rollouts per task, with learning rate 106 and temperature 0.7. Due to the page limit, we defer the remaining settings to Appendix A. Evaluation. The 155 evaluation templates include 132 ID templates with new task instances and 23 template-OOD templates. We train and evaluate under seeds 42, 43, and 44, which yield 465 evaluation episodes per model, run at temperature zero with fixed simulator clock. Success requires goal satisfaction and valid termination, and we also report goal satisfaction alone. We report the mean over the three seeds at step 16, and Tab. S1 in Appendix gives its mean and standard deviation across seeds. Evaluating in Full tests whether policy trained in reduced variant can operate when the original records and controls are present, as it must when deployed on real applications, so any mismatch between training and evaluation screens is part of the measured cost. Grouping evaluation by whether templates training environment was reduced shows whether gain comes from the modified tasks or from the others. 3 4. Which Construction Choices Hurt Performance? We lower each construction dimension in turn and evaluate the resulting policy in the full environment. Lowering reward or data coverage lowers success, whereas lowering feature coverage improves it. 4.1. Narrow Reward Suppresses Valid Solutions Table 1. Lowering reward coverage. Single-path reward tests whether accepting one anticipated solution costs policy that explores on its own. Under group-relative advantage, rejected success can be pushed down. At step 11 of alarm deletion, six rollouts delete the alarm through its edit sheet and one uses long-press selection. All seven succeed in three actions, and only the long-press path matches the reference. With one failure in the group, each edit-sheet success receives advantage 0.354 and the reference-path success +2.475. Native goal reward on the same samples gives all seven successes +0.354. Filtering records therefore costs where the filtered tasks meet real record lists, and the environment we construct later keeps all application records. It does the opposite (Tab. 3): F0 reaches 261/465 successes (56.13%) against 240/465 (51.61%) for Full, 4.52-point gain. F1, which keeps roughly half of the candidate functions, reaches 242/465. Gains Lie in Unmodified Tasks The F0 gain lies entirely outside the tasks F0 modified. We partition evaluation by the F0 masks  (Fig. 2)  into 61 affected templates, whose training environments F0 pruned; 71 unmodified templates, trained in identical environments under Full and F0; and 23 templates unseen in training. Full and F0 solve 97 and 96 of 183 affected instances, so pruning brings no net gain on the pruned tasks themselves. On the 213 unmodified instances, F0 raises successes from 101 to 128, while on unseen templates successes fall from 42 to 37. The net gain of 21 successes thus comes from tasks whose environments F0 never changed. Episode Length and Update Weight The F0 gain on unchanged tasks implies that pruning acts through the shared policys updates. Pruning changes training trajectories even with fixed task set and terminal reward. Episode contains Ti valid GUI responses and receives terminal group-relative advantage Ai, copied to each response. Each response can contain multiple text tokens. Under response averaging, the episodes raw coefficient exposure is proportional to TiAi. Twelve responses repeat an advantage four times as often as three, for either sign (Fig. 3, left). By changing the screens and actions the policy visits, function masks can change how much each episode contributes to training.

Under response averaging, F0 nearly preserves the target success count through late training. The step-12 start succeeds on 81/153 targets; F0 ends with 80 and Full with 62. Full loses 24 initial successes and gains five, whereas F0 loses 15 and gains 14, so F0s 18-success lead splits into nine more preserved and nine more newly solved instances. Paired trajectories illustrate how the interaction appears in behavior. For Railway ticket-price query, response-averaged F0 and balanced Full retrieve an order and answer in three actions, while the other two arms loop on date selection. Reading privacysetting task shows the opposite pattern: response-averaged F0 reaches the step limit while the other arms succeed. Appendix provides both examples and their selection rule. Appendix rules out two other explanations: F0 policies do not gain from being evaluated on the simpler F0 screens, and F0 does not lead before the unmodified tasks are practiced. Functional pruning therefore helps by preserving previously learned capabilities, and this benefit depends on how episodes on the pruned tasks are weighted by length. 6. Lite omits 87 templatemodule pairs across 72 of the 192 training templates: for these tasks, the corresponding functions need not be provided. Measured in lines of code, the application source pruned task needs shrinks by 14.05% on average over these 72 templates. Building in this style also costs less: we had Codex rebuild ten MobileGym applications, including WeChat and Bilibili, once completely in MobileGyms style and once implementing only the functions the main task templates use, close to F0, and the second rebuild used about 33% fewer tokens. On nine fixed screens, visible control nodes drop from 126 to 117, 7.14% reduction (F0: 113), while keeping the world-clock tab and the WeChat profile entrance  (Fig. 4)  . Lite keeps all 192 training templates and all application records. Appendix gives the per-screen measurements. 6.1. Construction Strategy 6.3. Late-Training Stabilization The study gives one rule per dimension. (1) Keep reward coverage complete: the verifier rewards any trajectory that passes the native goal check. (2) Keep data coverage complete: the environment retains every application record. (3) Lower feature coverage selectively: builder prunes dispensable functions and evaluates the pruned environment together with its training objective, since Sec. 5 shows that the objective decides whether pruning preserves learned capabilities. 6.2. MobileGym-Lite Selective pruning. Following this strategy, MobileGymLite rewards any trajectory that passes the native goal check, retains every application record, and prunes dispensable functions. It removes dispensable functions but keeps nearby navigation and shared operations. Starting from F0, it restores world-clock access for alarm tasks, Calendar settings for date-tool tasks, and profile editing for WeChat communication tasks. Alarm tasks thus keep the alarm and world-clock tabs but lose stopwatch and timer entrances, and communication tasks keep profile editing but lose Moments. These restorations affect 36 templates, six of which then retain all functions. Appendix specifies all profiles and restorations. Instability under reduction. Every reduced environment we trained, whether it lowers reward, data, or feature coverage, shows surge of loops and format errors late in training. From step 8 to step 16, loop terminations rise from 111 to 135 under R0 and format errors from 12 to 175 under R1, while Fulls loop terminations fall from 117 to 109. The pathrestricted policy ends with 144 loop terminations against 109 for its Full reference. Under feature pruning, success also fluctuates between checkpoints: F1 falls from 224 to 192 between steps 8 and 12 before recovering to 242, and Lite from 239 to 233 before recovering to 250. Narrow late clipping. We reduce this with one adjustment: after step k, the GSPO importance-ratio clip offsets narrow from the default 0.2/0.28 (lower/upper, W) to 0.002/0.0028 (N), written WNk. Branches share model and optimizer state at step 8 for Full, F0, and Lite (Tab. 6). The adjustment smooths Lites trajectory, from 239, 233, and 250 to 239, 242, and 258 at steps 8, 12, and 16, and raises its endpoint by eight successes. It leaves F0 at 262 against 261, and brings Full, which trains stably, no gain (238 against 240). Lite therefore uses WN8, and all other main-text runs use throughout. 7 Figure 4. Selective functional pruning in MobileGym-Lite. Full-screen screenshots use identical task states. Clock retains four tabs in Full, one in F0, and two in Lite. WeChat retains the profile card: F0 disables clicking and removes its chevron, and Lite restores both. Moments is removed in F0 and Lite. Circles highlight these controls, and dashed circles mark missing WeChat entrances. Table 7. MobileGym-Lite in the full environment. Success (%) over 465 instances. Both runs share settings through step 8; Lite narrows the importance-ratio clip thereafter (Sec. 6.3). Lite instantiates the construction rule rather than the highestscoring mask. Environment Step8 Step12 Step16 Full Lite 43.44 51.40 46.45 52. 51.61 55.48 6.4. Full-Environment Performance Success. Pruning speeds up learning (Tab. 7). Full and Lite train under the same settings through step 8, and Lite already solves 239 of 465 instances against Fulls 202, close to Fulls step-16 result of 240. At step 16, with WN8, Lite reaches 258/465 successes (55.48%), 18 more than Full (51.61%). Where the gain lies. Lite gains in all three evaluation groups: one success on the 183 affected instances, 12 on the 213 unmodified ones, and five on the 69 unseen-template ones. It solves 35 instances on which Full loops or exhausts the action budget, while introducing 14 such failures. Why Lite. F0 reaches 261 successes, three more than Lite. We release Lite because it prunes more conservatively: it restores three modules next to the tasks own navigation and disables 87 rather than 127 templatemodule pairs, and its gain holds in every evaluation group, whereas F0 loses five successes on unseen templates and one on affected ones. 7. Discussion and potential impact This study turns environment construction from engineering trade-offs into measured decisions, because the dimensions differ in what reduction removes. Leaving valid solutions unrewarded removes training signal and penalizes valid alternatives, and filtered records cost success where they return at deployment, whereas unneeded features mainly add detours. builder should therefore keep reward and data coverage complete and can lower feature coverage, spending the saved effort on more applications and tasks. The mechanism adds two criteria for judging reduced environment. Its gain appears on unmodified tasks, so multi-task environment should be judged by what the agent retains on other tasks, not only by what it learns on the reduced ones. The gain also depends on episode weighting, so pruned environment should be judged together with its training objective. Our reward-coverage study narrows the rewarded trajectories but keeps the transitions ; removing alternative routes from while keeping every task solvable is left open. We use one base model and one simulator, and replication across starting policies and simulators is the next step. 8. Conclusion less complete GUI environment need not train worse agent. What matters is which dimension construction choice lowers. Lowering reward coverage suppresses valid solutions, lowering data coverage lowers success on the filtered tasks, and lowering feature coverage improves fullenvironment success, entirely on tasks it never modified. The gain comes from length weighting on the pruned tasks: without pruning, long detour successes there are reinforced and erode tasks the policy already solves, and balancing only those tasks removes the gap. MobileGym-Lite applies these findings and reaches 55.48% success in the full environment, above Fulls 51.61%.

C), interface measurements (Sec. D), episodeweighting analysis (Sec. E), alternative mechanism checks (Sec. F), and paired examples (Sec. G). A. Tasks and Evaluation The study uses 192 training templates and 155 evaluation templates. The overlap contains 132 templates, evaluated with newly sampled instances, and the remaining 23 evaluation templates form the template-OOD set. Each template specifies an instruction, initial state, action budget, and executable goal checks. Environment labels identify available records/functions, and training branches also specify clipping and starting state. continuation restores saved checkpoint. We train and evaluate under seeds 42, 43, and 44. Table S1 gives the mean and standard deviation of step-16 success across seeds for Full, Lite, and F0. Task membership is fixed across the functional-pruning comparisons. The original F0 masks partition the evaluation set into 61 affected ID, 71 unmodified ID, and 23 templateOOD templates, giving 183, 213, and 69 instances. The mechanism studys primary retention set consists of 51 of Table S2. Shared settings for the functional-pruning and mechanism studies. An outer step samples 12 task instances, each with eight rollouts. These have all received practice by the common step 12 checkpoint and receive none in steps 1316. The remaining curriculum contains 48 templates: 19 affected and 29 others. Success requires native goal satisfaction and valid episode termination. We also report native-goal success separately in the mechanism study. Full-environment evaluation uses three seeds: 465 episodes per model and 153 on the retention set. B. Environment Construction B.1. Single-Path Reward reference is an ordered sequence of semantic operations tied to task instance. The bundle covers all 192 training templates: 139 references are semantic, 46 combine semantic operations with motor fallbacks, and seven use the historical motor representation. The 1546 retained operations include 181 motor fallbacks. Matching preserves operation order, route, and target identity. Equivalent purescroll chunks can be merged after replay, while unresolved motor targets use narrow observed regions. Private matching annotations are separate from the screenshots supplied to the policy. The learning effect of rejected success depends on its sampled group. For driving-cost query, six successful CLICK-then-TYPE solutions differ from the references direct TYPE, so all eight restricted rewards become zero, erasing the groups success/failure contrast. Birthday creation exposes sensitivity to an extra focus click and the save-button context. In Weather group, all eight valid solutions are rejected, but native binary success already gives zero relative advantage because all eight rewards agree. These cases separate reversal of useful credit, removal of reward contrast, and rejection without changed contrast. B.2. Record Filters Record filtering operates on reviewed lists of application records. protected set contains records needed by either branch of conditional task, its answer, alternate entrances, or shared helpers. R0/R1/R2 retain that protected set and up to 0/1/2 unrelated records per list. Retained rows preserve their complete fields, identities, and order. Filtering changes 78 training templates and leaves other templates unchanged. B.3. Function Profiles and Lite Restorations Function masks are unions of reviewed profile rules (Tab. S3). cross-application template may use more than one profile. F0 disables every candidate module in that union. F1 ranks S1 C.2. Template Groups and F0 Summary The fixed-group breakdown localizes the endpoint improvements (Tab. S5). Relative to Full, F0 gains 27 successes on unmodified tasks, loses one on affected tasks, and loses five on unseen templates. Lite gains 12, one, and five, respectively. C.3. Data-Coverage Results R0, R1, and R2 reach 223, 220, and 231 successes at step 16, against 240 for Full. C.4. Reward-Coverage Results The path-restricted run contains 1536 training episodes: 600 native successes, 348 reference matches, and 333 episodes satisfying both conditions. Outer steps 3 and 16 have zero group-relative advantage. Final evaluation gives 191 successes out of 465. The within-group cases in Sec. characterize how the single-path reward changes credit assignment. D. Pruned Interfaces The nine-view panel spans the function profiles listed in Tab. S7. All modes use the same task state, clock, and frontend. We render 360800 CSS-pixel viewport at device scale factor three, waiting for fonts and two animation frames after opening each view. Table S7 gives the counts, and Fig. S2 extends the main papers Clock and WeChat examples to Notes and Calendar. Table S6 summarizes functional coverage and the panel totals. The main figure preserves the full viewport and circles the relevant controls. For removed Moments entry, dashed circle marks the boundary between the remaining rows. Measurements use the original screenshots without annotations. counted control is visible viewport-intersecting DOM node matching tagged action/entrance, button, button role, input, textarea, or select. Multiple selector matches on one node count once, while tagged wrapper and an inner button count separately. Counts total 126 for Full, 113 for F0, and 117 for Lite, 7.14% reduction from Full to Lite on this panel. The measurement describes these selected views. Relative to the original Full environment, Lite reduces the application source pruned task needs by 14.05% of its lines on average over the 72 pruned templates, and it keeps all 192 training templates. To measure construction cost beyond source lines, we had the Codex coding agent rebuild ten MobileGym applications, including WeChat and Bilibili, in two styles. The complete style follows MobileGym and implements each application as fully as possible. The pruned style follows Lite and implements only the functions that the main task templates use, close to F0. The pruned rebuild consumed about 33% fewer tokens than the complete one. Figure S1. Because the weights are positive, scaling the advantage scales the responses clipped surrogate by the same factor. Token gradients and minibatch updates still depend on the responses that were generated. The implementation counts nonempty response rows by trajectory and episode identity, excluding padding. After terminal group normalization and broadcasting, it multiplies each rows advantage and return by C/Ti, while responsetoken averaging and minibatching stay unchanged. Both measures exhibit the same directional change. E.3. Update Contributions Table S10 summarizes the generated training episodes. Response-averaged Full and F0 have nearly identical success counts, 142 and 141 of 384, but F0 produces more GUI responses. On the 19 affected templates alone, Full/F0 have 57/60 successes and 1734/1915 responses. Thus the retention advantage accompanies changes in the distribution of trajectories even when aggregate training success is similar. We measure positive coefficient exposure as E+ = (cid:80) i:Ai>0 TiAi and negative exposure magnitude as = (cid:80) i:Ai<0 TiAi on the affected tail templates. Response averaging gives E+ = 386.2/320.3 and = 416.3/500.8 for Full/F0. Balancing replaces Ti by C, and its positive and negative magnitudes are 431.7 for Full and 464.8 for F0. The symmetry under balancing follows from group-normalized advantages and equal episode coefficients. These scalar measurements show which advantages are repeated more often, but their corresponding parameter updates also depend on token-level gradients. F. Additional Mechanism Checks F.1. Pruned Evaluation Context We test whether F0 prefers its training context by crossing fixed Full/F0 policies with Full/F0 evaluation environments. The comparison covers 61 affected templates and 12 unmodified controls at three seeds, for 876 episodes. The affected-task results give negative contextadaptation interaction. The Full policy succeeds on 101/183 instances in Full and 104/183 in F0 context, and the F0 policy succeeds on 102/183 and 98/183, respectively. The interaction is 7/183 = 3.83 points. Four outcome flips also occur on the unmodified controls, where the context switch changes no functions. On the affected tasks, switching to F0 context adds three successes for the Full policy and removes four for the F0 policy. F.2. Source-Only Transfer second check asks whether practicing pruned source tasks is sufficient to improve other tasks before direct target practice. We train Full/F0 pair on 72 source templates and then add common practice on 24 targets. Evaluations along this sequence contain 1410 episodes in total. Full has higher target success at both source-only checkpoints. Before target practice, F0 succeeds on 73/213 primary instances and Full on 81/213. After further source training, the corresponding counts are 89/213 and 95/213. The Full lead decreases from eight to six successes as source training continues. G. Paired Behavioral Examples We illustrate both signs of the environmentweighting interaction. Among the primary templates, we select the largest positive and largest negative interactions, break ties lexically, and take the first task seed with the corresponding sign. Table S11 summarizes the resulting two seed 42 instances. Ticket-price query. The Railway task asks for ticket price on specified date, and the answer is 58. Responseaveraged F0 and balanced Full open Orders, inspect the users tickets, and answer in three actions. Responseaveraged Full and balanced F0 instead open the date selector and repeat ineffective swipes until the nine-action loop stop. The step-12 starting policy also fails, repeatedly selecting an order entrance from the wrong page. The successful endpoints discover usable information-retrieval route on task absent from the training tail. Profile visibility. The Reading task asks to make profile visible to mutual followers. Response-averaged F0 misses the settings route and reaches the 30-action limit. The other three endpoints reach Settings, Privacy, and Profile Visibility, change the requested setting, and complete the task in 610 actions. This example shows that the retention benefit varies across tasks even within the same environmentweighting comparison. S
